source.title: Reasoning is Periodicity? Improving Large Language Models Through Effective Periodicity Modeling
source.authors: Yi Dong; Ge Li; Xue Jiang; Yong-Ding Tao; Kechi Zhang; Lecheng Wang; Hao Zhu; Huan-Yu Liu; Jiazheng Ding; Jia Li; Jin-Liang Deng; Hong Mei

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some figures are represented only by captions or flattened chart text, so their plotted loss values cannot be read from the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports language-modeling loss across model-size and training-token sweeps, testing scaling behavior with a different architecture and experimental setup from the original scaling-law studies.
record.gate_note: The scaling sweeps in Section 4.2 and Figure 3 report validation language-modeling loss as model size and training tokens vary. The appendix's 1T-token training-loss curves are not held-out loss results; the downstream benchmark comparisons and fixed-size ablations do not test the claim versions.
record.test_reason: An architecture paper (FANformer). Section 4.2's size and token sweeps compare FANformer's efficiency with Transformer. It fits no power law, reports no exponents and gives no readable loss values. It only asserts in one line that results 'align well' with Kaplan's law. Sizes span 268M–7B and tokens 20B–200B, roughly one order of magnitude each. The size sweep uses ~10B tokens, so the larger models are data-bottlenecked, against V1's condition. So the paper uses the scaling framing to present its own method rather than testing whether loss follows a power law.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors' central claim is that periodicity modeling via FAN in attention improves learning efficiency: FANformer beats Transformer when scaling parameters and tokens, with 31% fewer parameters and 20% fewer tokens for parity. FANformer-1B (1T tokens) beats comparable open LLMs downstream and shows better rule-based reasoning. They assert, without fitted numbers, that Kaplan's scaling law 'aligns well' with FANformer's results.
record.recipe_differences: The paper tests scaling sweeps for a modified attention architecture, comparing FANformer with Transformer and Transformer+ATM; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting procedure.

fits_no_version.finding: A modified attention (ATF) reaches Transformer-level loss with 69.2% of the parameters and ~79.8% of the tokens (159.6B vs 200B). The Transformer+ATM curve overlaps Transformer's.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture changes can shift the scaling curve by a constant efficiency multiplier, without the authors reporting any change to its form.

record.problems: The supplied text does not provide numerical loss values for the plotted scaling curves, fitted exponents, fit procedure, or uncertainty estimates. The parameter sweep spans 268M to 7B, and the token sweep is limited to 200B; the paper reports only one 1.1B model pretrained on 1T tokens.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were left out that directly test the listed claim versions. Appendix A's 1T-token curves report training loss rather than held-out loss; downstream task scores, architectural ablations at fixed size, and reasoning evaluations do not test these versions.

untested.parts: No fitted power law, exponents or readable loss values. Ranges are about one order of magnitude. The size sweep is data-bottlenecked at ~10B tokens. No compute sweep.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
Fixed-size architecture variants (Table 2) change the attention projection, not depth or width shape; they are not a shape test.
Downstream scores compare architectures, not trends with scale.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4. The scaling sweeps serve to compare architectures; the only scaling-law statement is an unquantified assertion. Minor inconsistency: the text says both 79.7% of tokens and a 20.3% reduction (159.6/200 = 79.8%).

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports validation loss trends for model-size and training-token sweeps, but does not report a compute sweep, fitted power-law exponents, formal fits, or evidence spanning several orders of magnitude in both sweeps.

rows.subject: FANformer
rows.operation_detail: Varied model parameter count and measured language-modeling loss.
rows.measure: Language-modeling loss across the model-size sweep
rows.baseline: Transformer; exact plotted loss values not stated in text
rows.note: The authors state that the scaling law empirically aligns with FANformer results and that FANformer consistently surpasses Transformer across the tested model sizes. They report comparable performance using 69.2% of the parameters required by Transformer.
rows.check: Figure-only, with no plotted values, fit or exponent. The size sweep trains every model on ~10B tokens, so 3B–7B models are data-limited, which violates V1's non-bottleneck condition. The 'observed' state rests only on the authors' one-line assertion. It is also unclear whether Figure 3 shows held-out or training loss.
